back: "The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing." The standard set of definitions for cloud computing. It also compares cloud services and deployment strategies.
open for public use.
used only by the client organization, either on-premises (on-prem) or in a dedicated area at a cloud provider.
shared between several organizations.
made of two or more clouds, which can include on-prem services.
you rent infrastructure and buy virtual power to run your software as needed. Like running a virtual server on a virtual disk. Similar to a utility company model, because you pay for what you use.

provides everything except applications. Covers all phases of the system development life cycle (SDLC) and can use APIs, website portals, or gateway software. Tends to be proprietary, which causes problems if the customer moves away from the provider's platform.
a complete packaged solution. The software is rented to the user, usually through a front end or web portal. The user can use it from anywhere, and the company pays a per-use fee.
a provider such as Azure, AWS, or GCP (Google Cloud Platform).
describes which security duties belong to the customer and which belong to the CSP. It depends on the service model. Amazon publishes one for AWS.
the contracted level of guaranteed service between the cloud provider and the customer.

front: DR/BCP (disaster recovery and business continuity plan)
back: how the provider responds to fire, storms, natural disasters, or power loss, and what continued service it guarantees.
development and project management method with at least five to seven phases in strict linear order. A phase can't start until the previous one is complete.
development and project management process that breaks a project into stages, with constant collaboration with stakeholders and continuous improvement and iteration at every stage.
the committed list of work in Agile.
what Agile teams turn an idea into, along with a feature specification.
a framework related to Agile. Teams learn through experience, self-organize, and reflect on wins and losses to improve. It defines a set of meetings, tools, and roles.
a short, time-boxed period in which a Scrum team completes a predefined amount of work. A key concept of Scrum and Agile.
management philosophy that eliminates waste of time and resources across the business. Agile is an implementation of Lean.
scheduling system for lean development and just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing, developed by Taiichi Ohno of Toyota. Agile uses it.
development method that improves quality and adapts to the changing needs of the customer, with iterative, frequent small releases. More commonly called XP; that abbreviation is not in the book.
stands for system development life cycle, and is also often used for secure development life cycle.

the convergence of many technical, project management, and management movements, built on Lean, Theory of Constraints, resilience engineering, learning organizations, safety culture, human factors, and more.
programmers merge code changes into a central repository multiple times a day.
sits on top of CI and automates the entire software release process.
each code change triggers an automated build-and-test sequence that gives feedback to the programmer. The goal is full automation, with each run logged and visible to the whole team.
quick sanity checks from the user's point of view, run first in a multistage test phase.
deployment environment used internally by the product team before production.

front: Serverless computing (FaaS, function as a service)
back: developers build and run applications without managing the server infrastructure. The cloud provider handles servers, virtual machines, networking, and scaling. Servers still exist; developers are just abstracted away from them.
a small, self-contained piece of code that performs a specific task. Usually event-driven.
one of the most popular serverless architectures. You run code without provisioning servers and pay only for the compute time you use. The book's figure captions spell it "Lamda."
bundles a program and its dependencies into a single artifact under a root file system.
each layer adds, removes, or modifies files from the layer before it. Each parent reference is a pointer.
one of the most popular container runtime engines. Packages an executable and pushes it to a remote registry for others to pull.
stores images. Offered by AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure, or run privately with open-source or commercial systems.
Docker's public image repository.
a file that automates the creation of a Docker container image.
the standardized form of the Docker image format, the most popular image format.
managing, deploying, and orchestrating containers.
one of the most popular container orchestration frameworks, originally developed by Google. Automates the distribution, scheduling, and orchestration of containers across a cluster.
container management and orchestration platform. The book says "HashCorp"; the company is HashiCorp.
a distributed Linux kernel with native support for launching containers with Docker and AppC images.
container cluster management and orchestration integrated with the Docker Engine.
Kubernetes component that coordinates all cluster activity: scheduling, scaling, and deploying applications.
a VM or physical server that acts as a worker machine in a Kubernetes cluster.
a group of one or more containers with shared storage and networking, plus a specification for how to run them. Each pod has an IP address and should be able to reach all other pods.
the official Kubernetes client. The book misspells it "kubctl" once.
Kubernetes component that bootstraps a minimum viable cluster and manages nodes in a multi-node cluster.
a lightweight Kubernetes implementation for learning.
GCP's hosted Kubernetes as a Service. Azure and AWS offer similar services.
network segmentation at the VM level or between containers, regardless of VLAN or subnet. Must be application aware.
open-source project for micro-segmentation policy-based services in container environments. Covered in Chapter 3.
moving security to the start of the development life cycle and building security practices into the CI/CD pipeline.
moving security earlier into design, coding, and testing.
make it easy for developers to write secure code and hard to make dangerous mistakes, with secure defaults in templates and frameworks.
OWASP's collection of secure development practices every developer should follow.
a software assurance method.
a software assurance method.

sends random data to the unit being tested to find input validation issues, program failures, buffer overflows, and other flaws. Works on applications, operating systems, infrastructure devices, IoT devices, and more.
a tool that performs fuzzing.
cloud-delivered solution that blocks malicious destinations using DNS. Evolved from the OpenDNS acquisition.
a suite of consumer products for a faster, safer, more reliable Internet.
all Umbrella data centers announce the same IP address, and requests go to the fastest, lowest-latency data center. Gives the recursive DNS service reliability and scale.
DNS technique botnets use to hide phishing and malware sites behind an ever-changing network of compromised hosts acting as proxies.
Umbrella's cloud-based proxy, which inspects only requests for risky domains.
a domain that hosts both malicious and safe content, usually because users can upload and share content. Examples: facebook.com, reddit.com, pastebin.com.
gives access to Umbrella's global intelligence to enrich security data and events and help with incident response. Through a web console or an API.

Cisco's cloud-based email security solution. Protects against ransomware, business email compromise (BEC), phishing, spear phishing, whaling, and other email attacks. The book uses this name for what its own figures and review questions call Cisco Cloud Email Security (CES). Not in the book: Cisco now sells Secure Email Threat Defense as a separate API-based Microsoft 365 product, and the gateway formerly called CES is Secure Email Cloud Gateway.
the operating system of Cisco Secure Email, Cisco Secure Web Appliance, and the cloud email security solution.
antispam engine.
detects spear phishing by checking parts of the SMTP message for manipulation, including the "Envelope-From," "Reply To," and "From" headers.
used for sender authentication.
used for domain authentication.

front: DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance)
back: used for domain authentication.
standards-based method to send and receive secure, verified email. Uses a public and private key pair to encrypt or sign messages.
industry term for proactively identifying and managing an organization's vulnerabilities and attack vectors in its digital ecosystem.

front: Cisco Attack Surface Management (formerly Cisco Secure Cloud Insights)
back: cloud-native platform that bridges gaps between separate security tools and gives visibility into risk across the whole cyber asset ecosystem.
on-prem analytics that uses NetFlow and context from the Cisco network. Covered in Chapter 5.
SaaS that identifies internal and external threats across on-prem, public cloud, and hybrid cloud environments.
virtual or physical appliance needed for Secure Cloud Analytics to monitor on-prem networks.
traffic across the perimeter.
lateral movement inside the network.
Cisco-acquired company. Gives end-to-end application visibility and performance insight, and builds a dynamic topology map of all applications.
Cisco agentless server application on a VM. Maps relationships between applications and infrastructure, anticipates performance and efficiency risks, and recommends actions.
uses rich traffic flow telemetry for data center use cases, with advanced analytics. Supports on-prem and public cloud workloads.
makes an outgoing connection from the orchestrator's network to the Secure Workload cluster, used as a reverse tunnel to reach the orchestrator API server.
Secure Workload function that gives insight into complex applications in a data center or in the cloud.
Secure Workload integrations for flow ingestion, inventory enrichment, and alert notifications.
per-minute aggregation of each unique flow in Secure Workload.
the two sides of a flow. The Consumer starts the flow and the Provider responds, like client and server.
aggregates telemetry from many security tools into central storage, analyzes the normalized data to detect malicious activity, and speeds response and remediation.

front: SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) and SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response)
back: earlier attempts to integrate disconnected security tools and reduce alerts. The book says they fall short.
Cisco's threat intelligence organization, used by Umbrella, email security, and XDR.
what Umbrella uses to block malicious destinations. UDP and TCP 53 is not in the book but worth knowing.

the message FED examines. TCP 25 is not in the book but worth knowing.

telemetry for Secure Analytics and Secure Cloud Analytics. UDP 2055 is a common NetFlow export port; not in the book but worth knowing.
